value.overview: The Black-cheeked Woodpecker (Melanerpes pucherani) is a small to medium-sized woodpecker of humid tropical forests in Central and northern South America. It is named for the dark cheek and facial markings that contrast with pale underparts and barred flanks. Males usually show more red on the crown and nape than females. This active species commonly forages in forest canopies, edges, and mature secondary growth, where it searches for insects, fruit, and nectar.
value.classification: The Black-cheeked Woodpecker belongs to the woodpecker family Picidae and the genus Melanerpes. It is closely related to several other tropical Melanerpes woodpeckers, including the Golden-naped Woodpecker.
value.identification: This woodpecker has a dark crown and cheek, a pale buff or olive-brown throat and underparts, and contrasting black-and-yellowish barring on the flanks and lower body. The center of the abdomen is often reddish. The upperparts are dark with pale spotting or barring. Adult males usually have a stronger orange-red crown and nape, while females have less red and a more extensively black crown. Its bill is dark and its legs are dull olive.
value.rangeHabitat: The Black-cheeked Woodpecker ranges from southern Mexico through Central America to western Colombia, western Ecuador, and locally into northern Peru. In Costa Rica it is a common resident of lowlands and foothills, especially along the Caribbean slope, generally reaching about 700 meters in the north and 900 meters in the southeast. It also occurs on the Pacific slope in and around the Cordillera de Guanacaste. Typical habitats include humid evergreen forest, forest edges, mature second growth, riparian woodland, clearings, plantations, and occasionally well-treed gardens.
value.migrationStatus: It is a year-round resident, not a regular long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica, individuals are present throughout the year, although local movements between forest patches and seasonal changes in abundance may occur.
value.breeding: Breeding in Costa Rica is reported mainly from March through June, with the broader breeding period sometimes extending into July. The pair excavates a cavity in a dead trunk or branch, commonly several meters above the ground and sometimes as high as 30 meters. Clutches usually contain two to four white eggs. Both adults participate in incubation and care of the young. Nest sites depend on the availability of standing dead wood and mature trees.
value.dietFeeding: The diet includes many arthropods, such as beetles, ants, spiders, and other insects. It also eats fruits, berries, seeds, and nectar from large tropical flowers. The bird usually forages alone or in pairs, working from the middle levels to the canopy. It probes, pecks, gleans prey from bark and foliage, and sometimes catches flying insects. Several birds may gather where fruit is abundant.
value.behavior: The Black-cheeked Woodpecker is active and agile, moving rapidly along trunks and branches and sometimes clinging beneath limbs. It may join mixed-species foraging flocks and occasionally visits gardens or open areas with scattered trees. Pairs may roost together in a cavity or separately. Calls include short rattling trills and sharper churring notes; both sexes can drum, though drumming is not especially frequent.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be decreasing, although the species remains widespread and is not currently considered globally threatened.
